structuredContent.title: ADR-0028: Always-on agent host — Postgres durability, inbox lease, CloudEvents envelope
structuredContent.text:
Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/41c830e8fbaa810fbf43d7912042d5ca as of 2026-11-18T19:12:25.559Z: {"title":"ADR-0028: Always-on agent host — Postgres durability, inbox lease, CloudEvents envelope"} null Status: Proposed Date: 2026-11-18 Decided by: Sven Maschek Issue: [SMA-785](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-785/adr-always-on-agent-host-durability-substrate-worker-model-event) Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-18-sma-785-agent-host-adr-design.md (paigasus-core, SMA-785) Builds on: ADR-0005, ADR-0006, ADR-0014, ADR-0016 ## Context - The article's model. Every trigger goes into a durable inbox. One worker per inbox merges the pending events into one run. Timers live in a separate store and never start runs. A scheduler turns due timers into inbox events. A run ends in one of three ways: send a message, send nothing, or defer a tool call for approval. - IAM already uses most of this pattern. ADR-0016: a Postgres transactional outbox (event_outbox, with attempts and parked), a relay that drains with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, NATS JetStream, and a CloudEvents 1.0 JSON envelope (rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/events/cloud_event.rs, extensions schemaversion, actorprn, correlationid). IAM uses SeaORM 2 with sea-orm-migration. - Helikon is a separate public repo (paigasus-helikon, published to [crates.io](http://crates.io)). The host depends on the published crates. Facts that this ADR builds on (verified in the code): - Sessions are an append-only SessionEvent log behind the Session trait (append, events, snapshot). A session id is a plain String. - TokioRunner calls snapshot() once at run start and append() once at finalize, also on a failed, cancelled or timed-out run. Persistence is best-effort: an append error is logged, not returned. run_streamed does not finalize on a natural end without a terminal event. - SessionRecorder::drain writes a synthetic result for every unmatched ToolCalled. It records the run input and four AgentEvent kinds only. Items that the loop adds to its own conversation are not recorded. - PermissionDecision is Allow | Deny | AskUser | Replace. Guard rules can return Ask. Both AskUser and guard Ask block the loop on an ApprovalHandler future. ApprovalOutcome is only Allow | Deny. LoopState::NeedsApproval exists and returns NotImplemented. - PreToolUse hooks run before authorisation and can replace the args. Replace can too. - The only mid-run control is a CancellationToken. Input guardrails run once, on the seed input. A hook can return InjectSystemMessage. Nothing can inject a user-role message. - CompactingSession compacts inside append, with a model call that nothing can cancel. Its summary is a SessionEvent::Compacted, which project() renders as Item::System. - TemporalRunner (runtime-temporal 0.5.3, Temporal Rust SDK 1.0) is implemented. Its v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs. - sessions-testkit (the Session conformance suite) has publish = false. - Helikon ADR-6: durability is a seam (Runner), not built in. - IAM has no delegation mechanism. A service cannot act for a principal today. Goals and anti-goals - Goal: one durability model for the inbox, timers, leases, runs, threads, sessions and the outbox. - Goal: at most one committed run per lease token, provable from the data. A run that lost its lease is cancelled at once and never commits. - Goal: one event envelope for every event that enters or leaves the host. - Goal: a rule that says, for every run, whether it resumes a session or starts a fresh one. - Goal: a deferred tool call that ends the run cleanly and resumes later. - Goal: a safe way for an event that arrives during a run to join that run, or to stop it. - Goal: a clear line between the open core and paigasus-cloud. - Non-goal: multi-agent coordination across inboxes (out of scope for v1, per the project description). - Non-goal: exactly-once delivery. The host is at-least-once with deduplication, like ADR-0016. - Non-goal: a Temporal adapter. The ADR keeps it possible. It does not build it. - Non-goal: a decision on how an agent holds a principal's access. See decision (k). - Anti-goal: the design fails, even if it works, if a self-hoster needs a Temporal cluster to run the core. - Anti-goal: untrusted content reaches the model in the system role (decision (n) lists every path). - Anti-goal: a crashed run sends half a message, or loses an event. - Anti-goal: two runs commit for the same inbox under the same lease. - Anti-goal: a party other than an authorised approver can approve a deferred call. ## Decision ### (a) Durability substrate: Postgres is the source of truth - The host's Postgres database holds every durable record: inbox, inbox_event, inbox_lease, run, thread, session_event, pending_tool_call, timer, outbox_message, and the Postgres memory store (SMA-789). - NATS is an ingress source (a JetStream consumer that writes inbox rows) and the fan-out for outbox events. It is never the source of truth for the inbox. - Redis is optional, for caches only. No correctness depends on it. - A Scheduler port in paigasus-agent-host-core turns due timers into inbox events (decision (l)). The core ships a Postgres adapter. A Temporal adapter can implement the same port later. - The core always runs Helikon's TokioRunner, through Runner::run, not run_streamed. The host does not wrap the loop in Temporal. Reason: TemporalRunner v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs, and the permission layer (SMA-793) needs hooks and guardrails. - Times that decide correctness (lease expiry, due timers, backoff) use the database clock (now(), or clock_timestamp() inside a transaction that can wait on a lock), never the worker clock. ### (b) Run lifecycle and the atomic commit Claim transaction (short, before the model loop): 1. Take the lease (decision (c)). 2. Select the claimable events of one thread (decision (f)). 3. Insert a run row: status running, the lease token, the claimed event ids. 4. Set claimed_run_id on those events and increment their attempts. Events keep the status pending. So a crash also counts as an attempt, and an expired lease frees the events with no reaper: an event whose claiming run is not running under a live lease is claimable again. No transaction or database connection stays open across the model loop. Commit transaction (one, at the end of the run), through a RunCommitter port in the domain (commit(RunOutcome, LeaseToken) -> Result), so the domain does not see SeaORM: 1. Lock the lease row (SELECT … FROM inbox_lease WHERE inbox_id = $1 FOR UPDATE) and check that token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp(). clock_timestamp(), not now(), because now() is the start time of the transaction and the commit can wait on the lock. The lock serialises the commit with a lease take, which updates the same row. A matching token on an expired lease does not pass, even when no other worker has taken the lease yet. 2. UPDATE run SET status = WHERE id = $run AND status = 'running'. Zero rows, or a failed lease check in step 1, means "already committed, or lease lost". Roll back and discard. This also makes a retried commit (a lost COMMIT acknowledgement) harmless. 3. Append the run's session events (PgRunSession, below). 4. Insert or update the thread row (last_run_at). 5. Insert outbox messages. Insert new timers. Cancel timers the run cancelled (for example an approval expiry). 6. Insert or resolve pending_tool_call rows (decision (g)). 7. Write the buffered memory changes of the Postgres memory adapter. 8. Mark the claimed and folded inbox events done. Outcomes. completed, deferred, stopped, failed, discarded. - failed: the runner returned an error. The host classifies it: - transient (provider 429 or 5xx, a database error): roll back. The events get a not_before backoff and stay pending. - deterministic (max turns, a guardrail tripwire, invalid structured output, a provider 4xx, a timeout): commit only the run row with the error. The partial session events are discarded, so a malformed session cannot poison the thread. The events stay pending. - After max_attempts, the events move to dead. The console shows dead events and can replay them (SMA-799). - discarded: the lease was lost. Nothing commits. - Every run has a maximum wall time (RunConfig.timeout). - final_output is never delivered to the user. Only the send tool (SMA-792) sends messages. The host stores final_output on the run row. PgRunSession contract. The host implements Helikon's Session trait itself, because sessions-postgres writes through its own pool and its own transaction. - snapshot() reads the committed events of the thread's session and projects them (with the compaction rule in (f)). - append() only buffers in memory. It never fails. - events() and snapshot() return the committed events plus the buffer. - The commit writes the buffer. If the run is discarded, the buffer is dropped. - The host runs Helikon's sessions-testkit against PgRunSession. Helikon publishes the testkit with the release that carries (g) and (h). Side-effect guarantee, stated as it is. A run commits once, at the end. If a worker crashes at turn 10, the next attempt runs turns 1 to 10 again. The model can make new call_ids and different args. So a side-effect tool is at-least-once per run attempt, with possibly different args. A deferral does not prevent a repeat: an approved call runs before the commit of the resumed run, so a crash there runs it again. An approved call keeps its call_id across attempts, because the call_id comes from the deferred run's log. A tool that must not repeat keeps its own idempotency check, on the business key or on that call_id. Messages to the user go through the outbox, so a re-run never sends them twice. The dispatcher itself is at-least-once: a crash after a send and before the delivery record can send a message again. It passes the outbox message id as an idempotency key to channels that support one (SMA-792). A per-turn commit would bound the repeat to one turn. It is not chosen for v1 (see Alternatives considered). The S3 memory adapter cannot join the transaction. Its writes are at-least-once and can survive a discarded run. The Postgres memory adapter is the default. ### (c) Worker model: one lease per inbox - inbox_lease (inbox_id PK, holder, token BIGINT, expires_at). Lease rows are never deleted, so a token never repeats. - Take the lease. INSERT … ON CONFLICT (inbox_id) DO UPDATE SET token = inbox_lease.token + 1, holder = …, expires_at = now() + ttl WHERE inbox_lease.expires_at < now() RETURNING token. This also works for a new inbox that has no lease row. The candidate inbox is selected with the claimable predicate of (f), with FOR UPDATE OF inbox_lease SKIP LOCKED when the query joins inbox_event. - Heartbeat. UPDATE inbox_lease SET expires_at = clock_timestamp() + ttl WHERE inbox_id = $1 AND token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp(). A heartbeat after expires_at does not revive the lease: zero rows means the lease is lost. lease_ttl is at least three heartbeat intervals. - Lease lost means: no successful heartbeat before expires_at. Zero rows updated and a database timeout both count, once expires_at has passed. On a lost lease the worker cancels the run at once with the CancellationToken and discards it. A cancel inside a tool call is no worse than the re-run that follows. - Interrupt. The run stops at the turn boundary (decision (h)), commits, keeps the lease, and claims again at once. Every claim under a held lease rotates the token first (UPDATE inbox_lease SET token = token + 1 … WHERE token = $t AND expires_at > clock_timestamp()), so the next run commits under a new token and the goal "at most one committed run per lease token" stays true. - One worker process serves many inboxes at the same time, up to a concurrency limit. ### (d) Inbox granularity, tenancy and routing - One inbox per (agent, principal). Split only when parallelism demands it (revisit trigger). - The inbox row holds the principal PRN. The org comes from the PRN (ADR-0014). Every query is scoped by the inbox. - An inbox is created explicitly, when an agent is bound to a principal. It is never created by the first event. - Routing. HTTP ingress names the inbox in the path (POST /v1/inboxes/{inbox}/events, SMA-787). Every other channel (a NATS subject, a webhook, an email address) has a channel configuration that maps it to exactly one inbox. An event that names no principal (for example an org-wide webhook) is routed by its channel configuration. A channel that cannot name one inbox is rejected at configuration time. - Ingress authorisation. Authentication alone does not let a caller write to an inbox. Before the insert, the host checks that the caller may write to the named inbox: a Cedar check through IAM (IsAuthorized, an agents action on the inbox resource) for HTTP ingress, and the channel binding for every other channel. A caller that fails the check gets 403, and no row is written. ### (e) Event envelope and ingress trust - Every inbox event, outbox message and approval reply is a CloudEvents 1.0 event in JSON structured mode (application/cloudevents+json), wire-compatible with IAM's cloud_event.rs (microsecond time, hyphenated id). - Extensions: schemaversion, actorprn, correlationid (as in IAM), and a new threadid. - data holds the proto3 JSON mapping of the agents/v1 message that type names. Events from outside (a raw webhook) carry their own JSON in data. type for events the host emits starts with agents. (for example agents.outbox.message). - Dedup. A unique constraint on (inbox_id, source, id). A duplicate insert is a success with no new row, and the handler returns 202. A duplicate whose payload differs is logged and counted. done rows are kept for a retention period, and that period is the dedup window. - The host, not the caller, sets the trust-bearing fields: - source comes from the authenticated channel configuration. - actorprn is the authenticated caller, set by the host. - A raw webhook without a CloudEvents id gets an id from the provider's delivery id, read from the header that the channel configuration names. A content hash is used only when the channel configuration selects it, for a provider whose identical payloads are always retries. Otherwise the host makes a new id, and that channel has no retry dedup. - A threadid is kept only if that thread belongs to the same inbox. Otherwise the host drops it, and the event starts a fresh thread. - Each channel configuration names how its caller is authenticated (an IAM API key, a webhook signature, a verified email sender). - The envelope code moves into a shared library crate (decision (j)). ### (f) Session policy: one run serves one thread - A thread is a sequence of runs on one Helikon session. The thread id is the Helikon session id. thread (id, inbox_id, created_at, last_run_at, closed, successor_id). - Every outbox message carries the threadid of the run that sent it. A user reply carries it back (the channel adapter maps it, for example from email In-Reply-To). An approval reply carries the threadid of the deferred run. - A thread is live when it exists, is not closed, and its last_run_at is within the thread TTL. A thread with an open deferred call is always live. An operator can close a thread. - The resolved thread. An event's threadid resolves through successor_id to the last thread of the chain. Every rule below uses the resolved thread, never the raw threadid. A run commit sets successor_id only on a thread whose successor_id is empty, so it never overwrites an existing link. (Storing the resolved id on the event is the builder's call.) - The claimable predicate. An event is claimable when its status is pending, not_before has passed, it is not claimed by a running run under a live lease, and one of these is true for its resolved thread: - the resolved thread has no open deferred call; - the event resolves that thread's open call: an approval reply that matches an open call_id, the call's expiry timer event, or a user message on that thread (see (g), "superseded"). A stale event of an older thread in the chain does not resolve a call of its successor.

The predicate is used both to select an inbox and to claim events. The open-deferral state is a column on thread, written by the run commit, and indexed. So an inbox whose only pending events wait on an approval is idle and is not selected again.

- Claim. Take the oldest claimable event of the inbox (by received_at). Group and order events by their resolved thread. - If its resolved thread is live, claim the claimable events with the same resolved thread, in received_at order, up to the batch limit. The run resumes that thread. - If its resolved thread is not live, claim the claimable events with the same resolved thread, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread, and the run commit sets successor_id on the resolved thread to the new thread. Events of two different expired threads never share a run. The rest of a backlog larger than the batch limit then resolves to the new thread and keeps its session history. - If it has no threadid (or the host dropped it, decision (e)), claim the claimable events that have no threadid, up to the batch limit. The run starts a fresh session under a new thread. If more such events wait than the batch limit, each batch is a separate session on purpose: an event with no threadid does not continue earlier work. - Events of other resolved threads stay pending for the next claim. So several messages in one thread still produce one reply, and no run mixes threads. - A timer event with a threadid follows the same rule. If its thread is not live, it starts a fresh thread. - Compaction is a host step, not CompactingSession. After a commit, under the same lease, if the thread's token estimate is over a threshold and the thread has no open deferred call: 1. Run a memory-flush turn, so that facts that must persist go to memory (SMA-791). 2. Write a summary as a Compacted event, made by a separate model call that the host can cancel. 3. PgRunSession::snapshot() projects a Compacted event as a delimited user-role item and drops the events before it. It never projects it as a system item. ### (g) Deferred tool calls Helikon changes (on #[non_exhaustive] types; compile-compatible for callers): - PermissionDecision::Defer { prompt } and ApprovalOutcome::Defer, so that a policy, a guard Ask and an AskUser can all defer. The host's ApprovalHandler returns Defer. One deferral answers every ask point of one call. - The loop uses the existing LoopState::NeedsApproval. When a turn holds deferred calls, the loop runs the turn's other allowed calls, records their results, and ends the run at the turn boundary. - RunResult gets a stop reason: Completed | Deferred { calls: Vec } | Stopped { reason }. It also reaches run_streamed consumers and agrees with AgentEvent::is_terminal. - PendingToolCall and a new SessionEvent::ToolDeferred hold the call_id, the tool, the effective args (after PreToolUse and Replace), and the active agent (for a handoff). SessionRecorder::drain does not write a synthetic result for a deferred call. - A resume entry point takes resolutions (call_id → Approved | Denied { reason }). It writes the results of all resolved calls before any new input. On Approved it runs the call with the effective args, on the recorded agent: - It does not fire PreToolUse again. - It runs the deny rules, guard Deny, the mode and the policy again. - Defer, AskUser and guard Ask count as answered by this approval. - Any Deny wins. - A Replace that changes the args denies the call. - A tool that the agent no longer has is denied with "tool no longer available". - A Defer inside an AgentAsTool sub-run (depth > 0) is a Deny in v1. Its session is discarded, so there is nothing to resume. - A runner that does not support Defer (for example TemporalRunner v0) treats it as Deny. - Core's own matches without a wildcard (SessionEvent::kind, ts, project, tool_exec.rs) change with the new variants. Once a tool_deferred event is stored, the host cannot roll back below that Helikon version, because an older reader cannot parse the row. Host side (SMA-795): - The run commits with outcome deferred, inserts one pending_tool_call row per call (state open), sets the thread's open-deferral column, inserts one expiry timer per call, and releases the lease. - One ApprovalRequest per call goes through the outbox. It shows the effective args. It carries the threadid, the call_id, a hash of the effective args (RFC 8785 canonical JSON), and an approval token (below). - The thread resumes only when every open call of the deferred turn has a resolution. The first resolution per call_id wins (a unique constraint). A later reply is marked done with the outcome stale. The resolving commit cancels the expiry timer. - States. open → approved | denied | expired | superseded → resolved. - Expiry. The expiry timer resolves the call as Denied { reason: "approval expired" }. - Superseded. A user message on a thread with open calls resolves every open call as Denied { reason: "superseded by a new user message" }. The run then continues with that message after the denial results. So "cancel that" works at once, and a thread never waits for hours. - Who may approve (accepted at Gate 1): only the inbox principal in v1. The reply endpoint authenticates the approver through IAM and checks that the approver PRN is the inbox principal. The approval token is single-use and unguessable: an HMAC over inbox_id, thread_id, call_id, the args hash and the expiry. An email link carries the token, opens a confirmation page, and the approver signs in there. The token alone does not approve. Delegates and admin approvers come later, with (k). ### (h) Mid-run events: a turn-boundary checkpoint Helikon change: - An optional callback on RunContext, called at every turn boundary of the top-level loop and of handoff children: after all tool results of a turn are recorded, before the next model call. It is never called inside a tool call, in an AgentAsTool sub-run, or at a boundary where a call was deferred. - It returns Continue | Inject(Vec) | Stop { reason }. - Inject content is user content. The loop emits a new AgentEvent for it, and SessionRecorder records it as a UserMessage. So the thread history contains it. - The loop runs the input guardrails on injected content. A tripwire ends the run with Stop. - Stop ends the run at the boundary with stop reason Stopped. No tool call is half done. Host side: - At each boundary, one indexed query reads new claimable events of the running thread. The host claims them under the same lease and the same run. - Each agent definition has a mid-run policy per event type: queue (the default), fold or interrupt. Approval replies and expiry timer events always use queue. Events of other threads are never read at a boundary. - queue: the event stays pending for the next run. - fold: the host returns Inject. The event is marked done in the run commit. If the run is discarded, the event is claimable again. - interrupt: the host returns Stop, commits the run as stopped, keeps the lease, and starts a new run on the same thread with the new events. - An operator cancel from the console (SMA-799) also returns Stop. The run commits as stopped and keeps its work so far. - An interrupt that arrives during the last model call does not stop that turn's outbox messages. v1 has no extra check before the commit. This is a known limit. - A TemporalRunner would need the same checkpoint later, as a workflow signal. That is outside this ADR. ### (i) Open-core boundary Under ADR-0006 (a published-artifact dependency edge): - Core (paigasus-core, Apache-2.0): the inbox, timers, worker, outbox and dispatcher; the webhook and email channels; the Postgres and S3 memory adapters; the Postgres Scheduler adapter; the agents console zone. - paigasus-cloud: managed channel apps (Slack, Teams), hosted dreaming, and any managed Temporal adapter. They use the published crates and the agents/v1 protos. They never patch the core. ### (j) Crate layout The project description's layout stands, with these additions: - A new library crate for the CloudEvents envelope (the name is the builder's call, for example paigasus-cloudevents). It owns parse, validate and build, with extension attributes per service, and keeps IAM's wire bytes unchanged. IAM moves to it in a later issue. This ADR does not require that move. - paigasus-agent-host depends on the published paigasus-helikon crates at a version that has (g) and (h), and on the published sessions-testkit as a dev-dependency. - Domain types in paigasus-agent-host-core: the RunCommitter and Scheduler ports, and PendingToolCall as an entity with the states in (g). ### (k) Acting for a principal: named, not decided IAM has no delegation or token-exchange mechanism. An inbox records which principal it acts for. How a run carries that principal's access is the subject of SMA-793 (permissions) and SMA-794 (the credential-injecting egress proxy). This ADR does not decide it. The approver rule in (g) does not depend on it. ### (l) The Scheduler port contract - Follow-ups (one-shot) and schedules (recurring, cron plus an IANA time zone) both exist in v1 (SMA-788). - A fire produces an inbox event with a deterministic id timer:: and a fixed source. The dedup constraint then makes a double fire harmless, for any adapter. - The Postgres adapter selects due timers with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, compared with the database now(). It inserts the event and marks the follow-up done (or advances the schedule) in one transaction. - A run commit can create and cancel timers. ### (m) Event-to-input rendering One renderer turns an inbox event into model input, for the first batch and for Inject: - The output is user-role content, never system-role. - Each event is a delimited block with its type, source, time and data. The delimiters mark the content as untrusted data, not as instructions. - actorprn, correlationid and other internal attributes are not shown to the model. ### (n) Paths into the system role | Path | Rule | | --- | --- | | Agent definition (system prompt, tool descriptions) | Operator-authored. The only system-role content. | | Helikon hooks with InjectSystemMessage | The host never uses them with event, tool or memory content. | | Compacted | Projected as user-role by PgRunSession (decision (f)). | | Memory loaded at run start (SMA-789, SMA-791) | Loaded as user-role content or as tool results, never system-role. | ### (o) Observability and crash tests - Metrics: lost leases, discarded runs, attempts per event, dead events, open deferrals and their age, inbox lag (oldest claimable event age). SMA-798 owns the names. - A crash-injection test matrix for SMA-790: after a tool call and before the commit; during the commit; after the commit and before the lease release; during a heartbeat partition. - A LISTEN/NOTIFY nudge, if added later, stays outside the run commit transaction. In IAM, a full notification queue fails the COMMIT. ## Consequences Positive - A self-hoster runs the core on Postgres and NATS. Redis is optional. Temporal is not needed. - A run that lost its lease never commits, and it stops at once. - A run's session events, messages, timers, deferrals, memory changes and inbox acks commit together, or not at all. - One run serves one thread, so provider message order and the thread history stay correct. - A deferred call is a first-class outcome, bound to the args the approver saw, and only the inbox principal can approve it. - Untrusted content never enters the system role, on any of the paths in (n). - One envelope across IAM and the agent host. Trace links (SMA-798) can use the CloudEvents id. Negative and risks - Two Helikon changes, (g) and (h), and the testkit publication come before SMA-795 and before the fold and interrupt policies. A delay in Helikon delays those issues. - After a deferral is stored, the host cannot roll back below the Helikon version that has (g). - The host owns PgRunSession and host-side compaction. They must stay correct against Helikon's session semantics. The testkit reduces this risk. - A crash repeats the whole run, so a side-effect tool can run again with different args. Tool authors must know this. - Polling Postgres for due timers and new events adds load. At high volume a nudge may be needed. - The S3 memory adapter is at-least-once and can keep writes of a discarded run. - An interrupt cannot stop the outbox messages of the turn that is in flight. ## Alternatives considered - Temporal as the durability substrate. Not chosen. Self-hosters would need a Temporal cluster. TemporalRunner v0 rejects hooks, guardrails and handoffs. The Scheduler port keeps it possible. - NATS JetStream as the inbox. Not chosen. The dedup window is time-limited, a work-queue stream gives no relational view for the console or for the claimable predicate, and timers and memory still need Postgres. NATS stays an ingress source. - Redis Streams as the inbox. Not chosen. Not durable enough to be the source of truth, and ADR-0016 already rejected it for events. - Postgres advisory locks instead of a lease row. Not chosen. A session-level lock is lost with the connection, gives no fencing token, and does not work well behind a pooler. - One inbox per agent, or per thread. Not chosen. Per agent mixes principals. Per thread loses one lease per principal. - A bespoke envelope, or binary protobuf. Not chosen. ADR-0016 already uses CloudEvents JSON. Protobuf stays an upgrade path. - One run for a batch with several threads. Not chosen. It puts user messages between tool results, which providers reject, and it sends replies on the wrong thread. - A per-turn commit. Not chosen for v1. It would bound a crash to one turn. But Helikon persists only at finalize, so it needs a third Helikon change, and it makes outbox messages of earlier turns visible before the run ends. Revisit trigger. - Helikon's CompactingSession. Not chosen. It projects the summary as system-role, compacts inside append before the commit, and makes a model call that nothing can cancel. - Session: one long session per inbox. Not chosen. Unrelated events share one context and compaction loses detail more often. - Session: always fresh, except approval replies. Not chosen. A normal reply loses the conversation unless memory holds it. - Defer: deny now, re-run later and let the model retry. Not chosen. It depends on the model sending the same call again, which is not verified. - Defer: block in the process until the answer comes. Not chosen. It holds the lease and a worker slot for hours. - Approval by possession of a link token alone. Not chosen. A forwarded email would approve a dangerous call. - Mid-run: interrupt only, through CancellationToken. Not chosen. A cancel can land inside a tool call, and a side-effect tool can then run twice. - Mid-run: a hook with InjectSystemMessage. Not chosen. It puts external content into the system role. ## Revisit triggers - Temporal's Rust SDK and TemporalRunner support hooks, guardrails and handoffs. - A principal needs parallel runs (split the inbox). - Postgres polling load becomes measurable (add a nudge, outside the commit). - Repeated side effects after crashes become a real problem (per-turn commit). - Helikon gets a native user-message injection API (re-check (h)). - Approval by delegates or admins is needed (extend (g), with (k)). ## References - [SMA-785](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-785/adr-always-on-agent-host-durability-substrate-worker-model-event): this issue - Anthropic, "Building always-on agents": [https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-always-on-agents](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-always-on-agents) - Helikon ADR-6 (durability is a seam): Library + pluggable Runner trait; durability is a seam, not built-in - ADR-0005, ADR-0006, ADR-0014, ADR-0016 - Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-18-sma-785-agent-host-adr-design.md (paigasus-core)

# Brainstorming

partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.
